fixes.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

Traditions play a powerful unifying role. Shared festivals, rituals and customs create a sense of collective identity and belonging, reminding people that they are part of something larger than themselves. They bring people together to celebrate or mourn collectively, strengthening social bonds. This shared heritage fosters mutual understanding and [[solidarity]]. In essence, traditions act as a kind of [[social glue]] that reinforces community [[cohesion]].
fixes.why: 'glue' alone is plain; marked the phrase 'social glue'

fixes.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].
fixes.why: 'relevant' and 'engaging' are plain; marked 'concerted effort' and 'artisans'
